# Whatever Comes to Me

I've been staring at this blank space for three minutes, which isn't very long in the grand scheme of things but feels significant when you're supposed to be writing. The cursor blinks. I blink back. It's a standoff between intention and inertia.

What comes to me first is always the meta-awareness that I'm writing about writing. Very creative. Very original. But here's the thing—maybe that's okay. Maybe the most honest thing is to just admit that the mind doesn't work like a faucet you turn on. It's messier than that. It's more like opening a door to a cluttered room and just describing what you see.

So what do I see right now?

I see the peculiar anxiety of the blank page. I see people everywhere—maybe you, maybe me—trying to figure out what matters enough to say out loud. I see the gap between what we think and what we actually type, that slippery space where meaning gets lost in translation from brain to fingers to screen.

I've been thinking lately about how we fill silence. We can't stand it, I think. Silence makes us uncomfortable, so we fill it with words, with music, with notifications, with the ambient hum of always being connected. But what if silence isn't empty? What if it's full of things we don't know how to name yet?

There's something about writing without a specific target—no argument to make, no point to prove, no audience in mind except the hypothetical you reading this—that feels both liberating and terrifying. It's like being told you can say anything, which paradoxically makes everything feel more important and less important simultaneously.

I keep thinking about the things I don't know. How little I understand about almost everything. How confident people sound when they talk about certainty, and how I mostly feel like I'm making it up as I go, hoping no one notices. I wonder if everyone feels this way or if some people actually have it figured out.

The human condition seems to be largely about pretending. We pretend to know what we're doing. We pretend we understand each other. We pretend that the things we worry about at 3 AM matter in the way we think they do in the daylight. Sometimes the pretending becomes so consistent that it turns into a kind of truth, but I'm not sure if that's wisdom or just another form of surrender.

What comes to me is also the strange gratitude for small things. The specific quality of light on an ordinary Tuesday. The way a dog can be completely present in a moment without wondering if they're wasting time. The fact that somewhere right now, someone is laughing at something genuinely funny, not at their phone, but really laughing. These moments exist alongside all the difficulty, like two transparent sheets overlaid on top of each other.

I'm thinking about how we're all just trying to figure out how to live. Some people do it through religion, some through relationships, some through art or work or nature or philosophy. Some people seem content with not figuring it out at all. Maybe that's the wisest approach.

There's something about writing that feels like archaeology. You dig through the layers of what you think you think until you find something that might be closer to what you actually think. It's rarely profound. It's usually simple things. "Be kind." "Pay attention." "Most of it doesn't matter as much as you think it does." "But some of it does." We keep learning the same lessons over and over, which is either deeply tragic or actually kind of beautiful.

I keep coming back to relationships—between people, between people and ideas, between people and their own selves. We're so hard on ourselves. We have this inner critic that would never speak to another human being the way it speaks to us. I wonder what would happen if we all just decided to extend to ourselves the same basic courtesy we extend to strangers. Not self-pity. Not delusion. Just basic human decency applied inward.

What comes to me is also the absurdity of existence. We're conscious animals on a rock floating through space. We know we're going to die, which is genuinely weird when you really think about it, but we mostly don't think about it because that way lies madness or at least serious discomfort. So we go to work and make coffee and text people and pretend that death isn't the ultimate fact of existence.

And yet, isn't that exactly right? Isn't that the only sane response—to acknowledge that it's all temporary and important and meaningless and vital all at the same time, and then just go ahead and live anyway?

There's freedom in that paradox if you can sit with it long enough.

As I near the end of this arbitrary word count, I'm aware of how this whole piece has been sort of shapeless. There's no narrative arc, no conclusion that ties everything together, no wisdom hard-earned and triumphantly delivered. It's just thoughts, scattered like papers blown across a floor. But maybe that's more honest than pretending to have it all figured out.

Maybe the real point is that whatever comes to you—if you're honest about it and patient with it—already contains something worth saying. You don't have to force it into a particular shape. You don't have to make it mean something grand. Sometimes just opening the door to the cluttered room and describing what you see is enough.

And if it's not? Well, at least we tried. At least we said something. At least we were here, making marks on the world, trying to communicate across the distance between one consciousness and another, which might be the most important thing we do.

That's what comes to me anyway.
